findings.claim: The model answer ranks Chaume Premier Cru below Bonnezeaux by concentration. It also says Quarts de Chaume has 'the region's highest must weight requirement at 298 g/L'.
findings.finalFix: ans: "Ascending by required must weight: Coteaux du Layon, then Coteaux du Layon followed by one of its named villages such as Rablay, Beaulieu, Saint-Aubin and Saint-Lambert; then Bonnezeaux, the enclave on the three hills above Thouarcé (at least 238 g/L, raised to 255 g/L in the 2022 revision, 25 hl/ha); then Coteaux du Layon Premier Cru Chaume (272 g/L, 25 hl/ha, successive hand-picked tries); then Quarts de Chaume, promoted in 2011 to the Loire's only Grand Cru (298 g/L and the lowest yield, 20 hl/ha). Coteaux du Layon Sélection de Grains Nobles sits apart as a mention, with the highest must-weight minimum of all at 323 g/L. Outside the Layon valley altogether: Coteaux de l'Aubance, on the little Aubance river between the Layon and Angers, and Anjou-Coteaux de la Loire, on the Loire itself around and above Savennières. All are Chenin, all on Armorican schist, and all depend on autumn mist off small rivers, the same mechanism as the Ciron at Sauternes on a smaller scale." accept[0]: "layon then bonnezeaux then chaume premier cru then quarts de chaume with aubance and anjou coteaux de la loire outside". accept[2]: "quarts de chaume grand cru at the top chaume premier cru below it"

findings.claim: The stem rests on a false premise. No Anjou AOP grows 'within sight of the Atlantic', and there is no '2011 appellation contiguity oddity'. The model answer is only '(Accept reasoned answers)', so the question has no gradable key.
findings.finalFix: Stem: 'Which Anjou AOP for dry Chenin Blanc sits on the north bank of the Loire just downstream of Angers, and is home to the Roche aux Moines and Coulée de Serrant crus?' Model answer: 'Savennières'. Accept: ['savennieres', 'savennières']. Explanation: 'Savennières (communes of Savennières, Bouchemaine and La Possonnière) lies on the right bank of the Loire west of Angers; it is well inland, not near the Atlantic.'

findings.claim: The model answer says the name Breton 'commemorates the Abbé Breton', Richelieu's steward in the seventeenth century.
findings.finalFix: Breton is the Loire's local name for Cabernet Franc. Tradition credits the Abbé Breton, steward to Cardinal Richelieu, with propagating the vine through Chinon and Bourgueil in the seventeenth century and so giving it his name. But Rabelais had already written of 'the good Breton wine' of the Véron by Chinon in Gargantua (1534), a century earlier, so the name is older than the Abbé and the story is legend. The DNA matters more than the folklore: Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc produced Cabernet Sauvignon, and crossed with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes produced Merlot; it is also a parent of Carmenère. In other words the Loire's grape is the ancestor of Bordeaux's, not a poor relation of them — the argument you make when someone calls Chinon a lesser claret.

findings.claim: The model answer says Vouvray and Montlouis are both 'one hundred per cent Chenin Blanc'.
findings.finalFix: Both are Chenin Blanc on tuffeau (Montlouis exclusively; Vouvray also permits a small accessory share of Orbois/Menu Pineau, now rarely used), and both run the full ladder from sec to moelleux plus pétillant and mousseux.

findings.claim: The model answer says 'Only Niagara Peninsula subdivides further'.
findings.finalFix: Below the provincial 'Ontario' appellation sit the Designated Viticultural Areas: Niagara Peninsula, Lake Erie North Shore and Prince Edward County. Lake Erie North Shore contains one sub-appellation, South Islands (Pelee Island, 2015). Niagara Peninsula subdivides into regional appellations (Niagara Escarpment, Niagara-on-the-Lake) and then ten sub-appellations, among them Beamsville Bench, Twenty Mile Bench, Short Hills Bench, Creek Shores, Four Mile Creek and St. David's Bench
